Take the positive square root of both sides: √49 = 7.
The radius of the circle is 7.
SAT-18#1: An arc is a fraction of the circumference, set by its central angle.
The fraction is 120/360 = 1/3 of the circle.
The full circumference of the circle is 2 × π × 6 = 12π.

SAT-18#2: Use the fact that π radians equals 180 degrees.
Replace π with 180 degrees, so the angle π/3 becomes 180 ÷ 3.

SAT-18#3: A sector is a fraction of the area of the circle, set by its central angle.

The full area of the circle is π × 10² = 100π.
One tenth of 100π is 10π, so the value of k is 10.
STAT-1#0: A categorical variable is a label or group name, even when it is written with digits. Ask which of these you would never average.
Shoe size, height and distance to school all measure an amount, so averages of them mean something.
A jersey number only identifies a player, and an average jersey number means nothing.
Jersey number is the categorical variable.
STAT-1#1: Relative frequency compares one category's count with the total: count ÷ total.
Tacos were chosen by 6 of the 20 students, so compute 6 ÷ 20 = 0.30.
As a percent, the relative frequency of tacos is 30%.
STAT-1#2: Skew is named after the side with the long tail, not the side with the pile of values.
Most games cluster at 0 to 2 goals, on the low side.
The tail stretches out toward 5 and 7, the high values on the right.
The long tail is on the high side, so the distribution is skewed right.
STAT-1#3: The words "of 10th graders" mean the whole is only the 10th-grade row, not everyone in the table.
Add the two counts in that row to get the 10th-grade total: 12 + 13 = 25 students.
In-person fans are 13 of those 25, and 13 ÷ 25 = 0.52.
So 52% of 10th graders prefer in person.
STAT-2#0: The median is the middle value, but only after the numbers are put in order.
Sorted from smallest to largest, the list is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
With five values, the middle one is the 3rd value in the sorted list.
The 3rd value is 5, so the median is 5.
STAT-2#1: The IQR is Q3 − Q1, where each quartile is the median of one half of the ordered data.
The lower half is 2, 4, 6, 8, and its median gives Q1 = (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
The upper half is 10, 12, 14, 16, and its median gives Q3 = (12 + 14)/2 = 13.
Subtract the quartiles to get the IQR: 13 − 5 = 8.
STAT-2#2: The outlier rule puts a fence 1.5 IQRs above Q3, so find the IQR first.
Subtract the quartiles to get the IQR: Q3 − Q1 = 30 − 20 = 10.
One and a half IQRs is the distance to the fence: 1.5 × 10 = 15.
The upper fence is 30 + 15 = 45, so any point above 45 is an outlier.
STAT-2#3: Standard deviation comes from the squared distances of the values from the mean.
The mean is 3, so the deviations are −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and their squares 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 add up to 10.
For a sample, divide by n − 1 = 4 to get the variance: 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5.
The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: s = √2.5 ≈ 1.58.
STAT-3#0: A z-score counts how many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
Subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation: z = (72 − 60)/8.
That is 12/8 = 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.
So a score of 72 has a z-score of 1.5.
STAT-3#1: The empirical rule gives three percents for a normal distribution: 68, 95 and 99.7.
They go with 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations from the mean, in that order.
Within 2 standard deviations is the middle number of the three.
About 95% of the distribution lies within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
STAT-3#2: The empirical rule says 68% of values lie between z = −1 and z = 1, and the two tails outside are equal.
The two tails together hold 100% − 68% = 32% of the values.
Half of that is in the lower tail: 32% ÷ 2 = 16% (a table gives 0.1587).
So about 16% of the values fall below z = −1.
STAT-3#3: A cutoff for the top 5% is a z-score turned back into a score: x = mean + z × SD.
Top 5% means 95% of scores are to the left, which is the given z = 1.645.
Turn the z-score back into an IQ score: x = 100 + 1.645 × 15 = 100 + 24.7.
The cutoff is x ≈ 124.7, so a score of about 125.
STAT-4#0: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value, in that order.
The actual score is 80 and the line predicts 81.5, so compute 80 − 81.5.
The residual is −1.5: the point is 1.5 below the line.
STAT-4#1: A regression line gives a prediction when you substitute the x-value into the equation.
Put x = 6 into the line and multiply first: 10 + 2 × 6 = 10 + 12.
The line predicts a y-value of 22 when x = 6.
STAT-4#2: Strength depends on how close r is to 1 or −1, not on the sign.
Ignore the signs and compare sizes: 0.9 is closer to 1 than 0.4 is.
So r = −0.9 shows the stronger linear relationship.
STAT-4#3: The percent of variation explained by the line is r², not r itself.
Square the correlation to get the fraction explained: 0.8² = 0.64.
So 64% of the variation in y is explained, and the other 36% is unexplained scatter.
STAT-5#0: A parameter describes a whole population, and a statistic describes a sample.

A number that describes a sample is a statistic, so 62% is a statistic.
STAT-5#1: Name a sampling method by asking how the people were chosen. Was any random process used?
The reporter simply talked to whoever was at the mall at that moment, with no randomness.
This is convenience sampling, which is biased toward people free at noon on a weekday.
STAT-5#2: Labels have two digits, so read the digits in pairs and skip any pair that is not a label from 01 to 30.
Split the digits into pairs from the left: 78, 03, 41, 19, 03.
The pair 78 is bigger than 30, so skip it and move to the next pair.
The first usable label is 03, so person 3 is chosen first.
STAT-5#3: In a systematic sample, the step size k is the population size divided by the sample size.
Divide the 2,000 names by the 100 wanted: 2000 ÷ 100 = 20.
So k = 20: take every 20th name after a random start from 1 to 20.
STAT-6#0: A treatment is one combination of a level from each factor, so count the combinations.
Each of the 2 fertilizers is paired with each of the 3 watering levels: 2 × 3.
That makes 6 treatments in the experiment.

Only random assignment of treatments balances out the confounding variables, and that happens only when the researcher imposes the treatments.

STAT-6#2: Ask how the students ended up in the tutoring group. Was anything randomly assigned?
Students chose tutoring themselves, so this is an observational study.
More motivated students may have signed up, so motivation is confounded with tutoring.
No, you cannot conclude that tutoring caused the higher scores.
STAT-6#3: In this kind of matched pairs design, each subject acts as his or her own pair.
The comparison is made within one person, so that person tries every treatment, in random order.
Each subject receives 2 treatments, which is both of them.
STAT-7#0: An event and its complement cover everything, so their probabilities add to 1.
Use the complement rule and subtract from 1: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.35.
The subtraction gives 0.65, so the probability of not A is 0.65.
STAT-7#1: The events overlap, so adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice. The general addition rule subtracts it once.
Write the rule with the given numbers: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) = 0.4 + 0.5 − 0.2.
The arithmetic gives 0.7, so the probability of A or B is 0.7.
STAT-7#2: Two events are independent exactly when P(A and B) equals P(A) × P(B).
Multiply the two separate probabilities together: P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2.
That product matches the given value P(A and B) = 0.2.
The test is passed, so yes, A and B are independent.
STAT-7#3: Without replacement, the second draw depends on the first, so multiply the first probability by a conditional one.
The first marble is blue with probability 2/5, since 2 of the 5 marbles are blue.
With one blue gone, 1 of the remaining 4 marbles is blue: probability 1/4.
Multiply the two steps: P(both blue) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 2/20, which reduces to 1/10.
STAT-8#0: The expected value is a weighted average: multiply each value by its probability and add.
Write one product for each value: E(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3).
The products are 0, 0.5 and 0.6, and they add to 1.1.
So the expected value of X is 1.1.
STAT-8#1: Adding a constant shifts every value but does not change spread. Multiplying by a constant stretches the spread.
The + 10 is ignored, and the 4 multiplies the standard deviation: 4 × 3.
So the standard deviation of Y is 12.
STAT-8#2: For independent variables, standard deviations do not add, but variances do.
Square each SD and add the variances: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25.
Take the square root to return to a standard deviation: √25 = 5.
So the standard deviation of X + Y is 5, not 3 + 4 = 7.
STAT-8#3: Expected net gain weights each possible net result by its probability, and the 1 dollar cost counts in every result.
A win nets 5 − 1 = 4 with probability 0.1, and a loss nets −1 with probability 0.9.
Weight each net result by its probability and add: 4(0.1) + (−1)(0.9) = 0.4 − 0.9 = −0.5.
The expected net gain is −0.5 dollars, a loss of 50 cents per play on average.

Each flip is heads with probability 0.5, and there is only one way to get all heads: C(3, 3) = 1.
P = (0.5)³ = 0.125, so the probability of three heads is 0.125, or 1/8.
STAT-9#1: The mean of a binomial variable is the number of trials times the probability of success: μ = np.
Here there are n = 100 trials with success probability p = 0.2, so compute 100 × 0.2.
The mean of the binomial variable is 20.
STAT-9#2: Waiting for the first success is a geometric setting, and its mean is 1/p.
The chance of a win on each card is p = 0.25, so compute 1 ÷ 0.25.
On average it takes 4 cards to get the first win.
STAT-9#3: Use the binomial idea: count the orderings with exactly 2 heads, then multiply by the probability of one ordering.
There are C(6, 2) = 15 ways to choose which two flips are heads.
Each specific sequence of six flips has probability (0.5)⁶ = 1/64.
Multiply the count by that probability: 15 × 1/64 = 15/64, which is about 0.234.
STAT-10#0: Sample means vary less than individual values: the standard deviation of x̄ is σ/√n.
Substitute the population SD of 20 and the sample size of 25: 20/√25 = 20/5.
So the standard deviation of the sample mean is 4.
STAT-10#1: The standard deviation of a sample proportion is √(p(1 − p)/n).
Substitute p = 0.5 and n = 100 under the square root: √(0.5 × 0.5 / 100) = √0.0025.
So the standard deviation of the sample proportion is 0.05.
STAT-10#2: This is about a sample mean, so standardize with the standard deviation of x̄, which is σ/√n.
The standard deviation of the sample mean is 15/√9 = 5.
Standardize 110 with that smaller standard deviation: z = (110 − 100)/5 = 2.
The area above z = 2 is 0.0228, so the probability that the sample mean is over 110 is 0.0228.
STAT-10#3: The standard deviation of x̄ is σ/√n, so it shrinks with the square root of the sample size.
To halve it, √n must double, which means n must be 4 times as large.
Multiply the old sample size by 4: the new sample size is 4 × 20 = 80.

The standard error of the sample proportion is √(0.5 × 0.5 / 100) = 0.05.
For 95% confidence the critical value is z* = 1.96, so ME = 1.96 × 0.05.
The margin of error is 0.098, or about 0.10.
STAT-11#1: For a mean, the margin of error is t* times the standard error s/√n.
The standard error of the sample mean is 6/√9 = 2.
Multiply by the critical value: ME = 2.262 × 2 = 4.524.
The margin of error is about 4.52.
STAT-11#2: A confidence interval is p̂ ± margin of error, so p̂ sits exactly in the middle of the interval.
Find the midpoint by averaging the endpoints: (0.42 + 0.50)/2.
The midpoint is 0.46, so the sample proportion was 0.46.
STAT-11#3: With no guess for p, use the worst case p = 0.5, and solve the margin of error formula for n.
With those numbers the formula becomes n = (1.96/0.05)² × 0.25, which is (39.2)² × 0.25.
Squaring and then multiplying gives 1536.64 × 0.25 = 384.16 people.
Sample size must be a whole number that is big enough, so round up to 385.

Use p = 0.5 from the null hypothesis in the standard deviation: √(0.5 × 0.5 / 100) = 0.05.
Divide the gap between the sample proportion and 0.50 by it: (0.55 − 0.50)/0.05 = 0.05/0.05.
The division gives 1, so the z statistic is 1.0.
STAT-12#1: The t statistic is the distance from x̄ to the null mean, divided by the standard error s/√n.
The standard error of the sample mean is 10/√25 = 2.
Divide the gap between the sample mean and 50 by it: (52 − 50)/2 = 2/2.
The division gives 1, so the t statistic is 1.0.
STAT-12#2: The decision rule compares the p-value with the significance level α.
Here the p-value 0.03 is at or below α = 0.05, so the result would be unlikely if H0 were true.
The evidence is strong enough, so the decision is to reject H0.
STAT-12#3: A Type I error means rejecting H0 when H0 is actually true.
H0 is rejected exactly when the p-value is at or below α, and when H0 is true that happens with probability α.
So the probability of a Type I error is α = 0.01.
STAT-13#0: The pooled proportion treats the two groups as one big sample: total successes over total sample size.
Add the successes and add the sizes: (40 + 20)/(80 + 80) = 60/160.
The pooled proportion is 0.375, which is 3/8.
STAT-13#1: Each cell contributes (observed − expected)² divided by expected to the chi-square statistic.
Substitute the observed count 30 and the expected count 25: (30 − 25)²/25 = 25/25.
This cell's contribution to chi-square is 1.
STAT-13#2: For a test of independence, the degrees of freedom are (rows − 1) × (columns − 1).
The table has 3 rows and 4 columns, so compute (3 − 1)(4 − 1) = 2 × 3.
The test has 6 degrees of freedom.
STAT-13#3: For two independent samples, the standard error of the difference adds the two variance terms under one square root.
Square each standard deviation and divide by its sample size: 6²/36 = 36/36 and 8²/64 = 64/64.
Each term equals 1, so the sum under the square root is 1 + 1 = 2.
The standard error of the difference is √2, which is about 1.41.
STAT-14#0: The t statistic for a slope is the estimate minus the null value, divided by its standard error.
The null value is 0, so t = b/SE_b = 3.0/1.5.
The slope is 2 standard errors from zero, so the t statistic is 2.
STAT-14#1: Inference for a regression slope uses df = n − 2, because the slope and the intercept are both estimated.
There are 22 data points, so subtract 2 from 22.
The slope test has 20 degrees of freedom.
STAT-14#2: The margin of error is the critical value times the standard error of the slope: ME = t* × SE_b.
Substitute the critical value and the standard error: 2.101 × 0.60 = 1.2606.
The margin of error is about 1.26.
STAT-14#3: To predict from a regression line, substitute the x-value into the equation.
Put x = 5 into the line and multiply before adding: 12.5 + 2.4 × 5 = 12.5 + 12.
The line predicts a score of 24.5 for 5 hours.

Add one full turn to the angle: −120 + 360.
The sum is 240, so the positive coterminal angle is 240°.

360 ÷ 60 = 6, so the minute hand turns 6° each minute.
TRIG-2#0: A half turn is 180° and also π radians, so degrees become radians when you multiply by π/180.
Multiply the angle by the factor: 60 × π/180 = 60π/180.
Divide top and bottom by 60 to simplify, which gives π/3 radians.

Put in the radius 6 and the angle 3 radians: s = 6 × 3.
6 × 3 = 18, so the length of the arc is 18 m.
TRIG-2#3: With the angle in radians, the area of a sector is A = ½r²θ.

The opposite side is 3 and the hypotenuse is 5, so write 3 over 5.
So sin θ = 3/5, which is 0.6 as a decimal.
TRIG-3#1: Cosine is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse (CAH), so decide which length plays each role.
The 5 m along the ground touches the angle, so it is adjacent, and the 13 m ladder is the hypotenuse.
